### page_1
Paleomagnetism of Archean granites and Matachewan dikes in the Wawa 
Subprovince, Ontario: reevaluation of the Archean apparent polar wander path1 
T. A. VANDALL' AND D. T. A. SYMONS 
Department of Geology, Universiw of Windsor, Windsor, Ont., Canada N9B 3P4 
Received October 10, 1989 
Revision accepted March 30, 1990 
Paleomagnetic measurements have been completed on 400 specimens from dated Archean granites and Matachewan dikes 
in the Michipicoten and Gamitagama greenstone belts in the western Wawa Subprovince of the Superior Province, Ontario. 
Detailed alternating-field and thermal step demagnetization analyses were used to isolate stable remanence directions. A 
single-component remanence was isolated within three adjacent dated granitic plutons on the eastern margin of the Michipicoten 
belt, including the Hawk Lake trondhjernite, the Southern external granite, and the Eastern external granite (HSE). The maximum 
possible age for this remanence is constrained by the intrusion of the last pluton at 2694 Ma. The corresponding HSE paleopole 
is located at low, 41"s (dp = 8", dm = 13"). A second paleopole, NB, is derived from the Northern external granite and the 
Baldhead River quartz monzonite, which give U-Pb zircon ages of 2662 and 2668 Ma, respectively. Their single-component 
remanence defines a paleopole on the Archean apparent polar wander path (APWP) at 15OE, 27"s (dp = 8", dm = 13"), with a 
maximum possible age of 2.66 Ga. A third paleopole, GD, is derived from the north-northwest-trending Gamitagama diabase 
dikes and yields a position of 57"E, 41W (dp = 7", dm = 14"), which agrees with poles determined by other workers from the 
2454 Ma Matachewan dike swarm. The GD pole, along with previously determined Matachewan dike poles, demonstrates that a 
tectonically stable craton has existed since intrusion of this extensive dike swarm, and it improves the precision of the 2454 Ma 
Matachewan pole on the APWP. These poles, when compared with coeval poles from the eastern side of the Kapuskasing 
Structural Zone in the Superior Province, imply no tectonic rotation or translation between the Wawa and Abitibi subprovinces 
along this Early Proterozoic structure.

Can. J. Earth Sci. 27, 1031-1039 (1990) [Traduit par la revue] 
Introduction 
To date there are relatively few paleopoles determined for 
Archean rock units in the North American Shield, and most of 
these are poorly dated. As a result, the acquisition times for their 
remanent magnetizations are even more poorly known. Thus, 
the Archean apparent polar wander paths (APWP) that have 
been constructed for North America (e.g., Irving and Naldrett 
1977; Irving 1979; Seguin et al. 1983; Dunlop 1984a) are for 
the most part based on paleopoles with large error limits on their 
ages. This age problem was demonstrated most recently when a 
more precise U-Pb zircon age for the Matachewan-Hearst 
dikes of 2454 2 2 Ma was detennined (Heaman 1988), replacing 
the previous Rb-Sr isochron age of 2633 +- 91 Ma (Gates and 
Hurley 1973; Easton 1986). 
In this paper we describe new paleomagnetic results from 
U-Pb-dated granites and dikes in the Wawa Subprovince of the 
ar it hop robe Publication 162 from the Kapuskasing Structural Zone 
transect. 
'present address: Department of Geophysics, The University of 
Western Ontario, London, Ont., Canada N6A 5B7. 
Superior Province. Our purpose was to define paleopoles from 
the Wawa Subprovince for the APWP and thereby see if there 
has been significant post-Archean translation and (or) rotation 
on the Kapuskasing Structural Zone (KSZ), as has been 
postulated (e.g., Bennett et al. 1967; Watson 1980; Ernst and 
Halls 1984). 
Geology 
The Michipicoten and Gamitagama greenstone belts are located 
in the western part of the volcanic-rich Wawa Subprovince 
of the Archean Superior Province. They have experienced 
greenschist-grade metamorphism and are separated by an 
intervening granitic terrane. Both are typical Archean green- 
stone belts, being comprised mostly of mafic to felsic metavol- 
canic flows and pyroclastics with interbedded metasediments 
(Ayres 1969; Sage 1979; Attoh 1980). These strata have been 
intruded by a number of granitic and gabbroic dikes, sills, 
stocks, and plutons that are likely subjacent intrusive equiva- 
lents of the extrusive rocks (Ayres 1969). Surrounding the 
greenstone belts are regional masses of granite and granitic 
gneiss that make up the external granitic terrane. From U-Pb

### page_2
1032 CAN. J. EARTH SCI. VOL. 27, 1990 
FIG. 1. Michipicoten and Gamitagama greenstone belts with their 
age date localities (after Turek et al. 1984) and the paleomagnetic 
sites. The Northern external granite sites (19-24) are shown by the 
closed rectangle and the Baldhead River quartz monzonite sites by 
the closed circles (NB); the combined Hawk Lake trondhjemite, 
Southern external granite, and Eastern external granite sites (HSE), 
by the closed squares; and the Gamitagama dike sites (GD), by the 
closed triangles. BR, Baldhead River quartz monzonite; GL, Gamita- 
gama Lake complex. Both BR and GL are enclosed by greenstones. 
zircon geochronology Turek et al. (1984) determined that the 
volcanism in these belts extended from at least 2749 to 2696 Ma 
and that the plutonism extended from at least 2888 to 2615 Ma. 
Transecting all older rock units are the Matachewan and the 
Abitibi dike swarms, which trend north-northwest and north- 
east, respectively. 
Methods 
The external granitic terrane was sampled in three abutting 
plutons on the east side of the Michipicoten Belt, namely, the 
Hawk Lake trondhjemite (2747 + 7 Ma), the Southern external 
granite (2694 + 3 Ma), and the Eastern external granite (2888 + 
2 Ma) (Turek et al. 1982, 1984) (HSE sites 25-40; Fig. 1). Also 
sampled were the Northern external granite (2662 2 5 Ma) and 
the Baldhead River quartz monzonite (2668 + 2 Ma) (NB sites 
10-24) and the north-northwest-trending Gamitagama diabase 
dikes, which are part of the Matachewan dike swarm (2454 2 2 
Ma) (Krogh and Turek 1982; Turek et al. 1984; Heaman 1988) 
(GD sites 1-9; Fig. 1). 
At least five core samples were drilled and oriented in situ by 
magnetic and solar compass at each of the 40 sites. Two 
specimens were cut from each core. The specimens were ana- 
lyzed inside a magnetically shielded room using a Schonstedt 
SSM-1A spinner magnetometer, CTF cryogenic magnetometer, 
Schonstedt GSD- 1 AF demagnetizer, and Schonstedt TSD- 1 
thermal demagnetizer. After measuring the natural remanent 
magnetization (NRM), two independently oriented specimens 
per site were demagnetized in 11 or 12 steps (selected from steps 
5,10,15,20,21,27,30,35,40,45,50,55,60,70,85, and99; 
units in mT) by alternating fields (AF's) to 99 mT. A further two 
independently oriented specimens per site were thermally 
demagnetized in 11 or 12 steps (selected from steps 22, 100, 
200, 300, 400, 450, 500, 525, 545, 575, 600, 625, 640, and 
650; units in "C) to 650°C. Orthogonal vector decay plots 
indicated that single stable components were isolated after 
demagnetization removed the "soft" remanence residing in low- 
coercivity , low-laboratory-unblocking-temperature domains. 
Directions were obtained by a joint analysis of stereographic 
plots, orthogonal demagnetization diagrams, and principal- 
component analysis (Kirschvink 1980). Directions of remanence 
were accepted with a mean angular deviation (MAD) < 10". The 
remaining specimens from each site were demagnetized using a 
combination of four AF steps and one thermal step, which 
varied for each site depending on the detailed step demagnetiza- 
tion behavior (selected from AF steps 10, 15, 20, 21, 27, 30, 
35, 55, 70, 85, and 99 (units in mT) and thermal step 500°C). 
Site mean remanence directions were calculated using conven- 
tional tiered statistics (Fisher 1953; Irving 1964). 
Ten specimens, representing each of the major lithologies 
sampled, were subjected to saturation isothermal remanent 
magnetization (SIRM) analysis to characterize their magnetic 
remanence carriers. 
Results 
All accepted specimen directions displayed single-component 
demagnetization vectors after the initial removal of soft viscous 
remanence components by about 15 mT or 300°C. Orthogonal 
vector decay plots are shown in Fig. 2 for each of the rock units 
in which its characteristic remanence direction is isolated. For 
both the HSE and NB group sites, antiparallel polarity direc- 
tions were isolated (Figs. 2b, 2d-2J). Alternating-field demag- 
netization produced better results for all of the analyzed rock 
units and isolated their characteristic remanences in domains 
with coercivities up to 99 mT (Figs. 2b-2d, 2f). Examples of 
stable thermal step-demagnetized specimen directions from units 
NB and HSE are shown in Figs. 2a and 2e, respectively. How- 
ever, the external granites in general and the diabase dikes in 
particular did not respond well to thermal demagnetization, 
which isolated the same components but in fewer specimens and 
with poor precision. As is often found in Archean rocks, espe- 
cially granites, many of the specimens displayed erratic unstable 
remanence directions on demagnetization. The rejection of 
these data from these specimens led to low N values for several 
sites in Table 1. Site mean directions with ag5's > 35" were 
considered unstable and, therefore, were rejected from unit 
mean calculations. One could argue for a more conservative site 
mean acceptance criteria of ag5's < 20". However, the unit 
mean directions would change by negligeable amounts except 
for a small decrease in precision because of the smaller numbers 
of sites. In addition, all accepted site mean directions were 
tested for randomness by comparing the calculated R value with 
the tabulated significance point R, for different values of N 
(Irving 1964). This test demonstrated that our accepted site

means have a greater than 95% probability that their directions 
have not arisen by chance and are therefore significant for 
directional studies of the paleomagnetic field. Although the data 
from site 5 pass this test, they were rejected because their 
remanence directions were best grouped at only 10 mT and thus 
were likely to have retained undemagnetized viscous com- 
ponents. Thus, only those sites with (Y~~'s < 35O, excluding 
site 5, were used to calculate the three unit means (Table 2). 
Although some of the site mean dispersions are relatively high 
in the granite rocks, this is expected because these are relatively 
coarse-grained rocks that contain a smaller percentage of 
ferromagnetic minerals. 
Both magnetic polarities were observed in all of the sampled 
rock units except for the diabase dikes, which retained only one 
polarity. By convention, all specimen directions with negative 
inclinations were converted to their antipodal positive directions 
to calculate the unit means except for the diabase dikes (Fig. 3). 
Each unit shows a good cluster of site means, with a degree of 
directional dispersion that can be reasonably attributed to 
secular variation. 
It is important to observe that the site mean directions of the 
granitic rocks-in particular the NB group, which includes data 
from the Baldhead River quartz monzonite (BRQM)-are very 
different from the diabase dike site means (Fig. 3). Seven of the 
nine sampled diabase dikes physically intrude the BRQM, 
which yields a markedly different remanence direction, provid- 
ing a positive contact test (Fig. 1). Therefore, it is unlikely that a 
post-Matachewan remagnetization event could have reset the 
magnetization of these granitic rocks without also having reset 
the Matachewan dike remanence. Thus, in all probability the 
magnetizations from the granitic rocks predate the Matachewan 
dike remanence.

HSE specimens show a variety of behaviors (Fig. 4a). Speci-

men a shows only multidomain (MD) magnetite behavior. 
Specimens b-d show the rapid initial remanence acquisition 
characteristic of some MD magnetite content, with a subsequent 
slower rate of acquisition that is indicative of predominantly 
pseudosingle-domain (PSD) to single-domain (SD) magnetite. 
In addition, specimen d appears to have a significant hematite 
content, denoted by the slow continued remanence acquisition 
above 0.3 T. Specimens e and f have PSD to SD magnetite 
behavior and also appear to have some hematite content. Both 
specimens g and h from the NB granite group have curves that 
indicate the dominance of PSD to SD magnetite, with specimen 
g having a little MD magnetite also (Fig. 4b). Finally, 
specimens i and j from the GD diabase dike group both show 
typical MD magnetite behavior only. As expected from samples 
of different lithologies, there are a variety of magnetic carriers 
within the sampled units. In general, the sites with the greatest 
dispersion in remanence direction, as measured by larger agg9s 
(Table I), are also those with the most variable combination of 
carriers. 
Discussion 
The Archean APWP for North America, as pointed out by 
Roy (1983), is based on a nonsystematic sampling of a noncon- 
tinuous paleomagnetic record. This is a fundamental problem

FIG. 3. Lower hemisphere stereographic projections of site mean 
remanence directions. Closed symbols are of positive (down) polarity, 
open symbols of negative (up) polarity. (a) HSE site means and unit 
mean, with the present Earth's magnetic field (PEMF). (b) NB and GD

polarities (Table 1); thus their negative polarities have been converted 
to their antipodal positive direction. 
that paleomagnetists can do little about, especially in the 
Precambrian. Roy (1983) also noted that the magnetization age 
of only a few poles was known to within &50 Ma and that for 
many the error was more than a100 Ma. Thus the Archean 
APWP's that have been constructed for North America by Irving 
and Naldrett (1977), Irving (1979), Seguin et al. (1983), and 
Dunlop (1984~) are based for the most part on paleopoles with 
large error limits on their ages. Recently, the U-Pb zircon 
dating method has contributed much more precise age dates for 
many rock units in the Superior Province, in turn establishing 
maximum ages for the magnetizations of many Archean poles, 
including those determined in this study. 
Also, there are tectonic problems. Hoffman (1988) has pro- 
vided a model for the assembly of the Archean cratons that 
form the Precambrian Shield of North America. In his model the 
Archean Slave and Superior cratons are united into one plate 
during the Proterozoic by collision to form the intervening trans- 
Hudson orogen. Dunsmore and Symons (1990) argued from 
palmmagnetic data that the intervening ocean was about 4000 km 
wide and it closed in the formation of the orogen, and thus 
they have confirmed earlier suggestions that the Slave and 
Superior provinces require separate APWP's before 1750 Ma 
(e.g., Cavenaugh and Seyfert 1977; Irving et al. 1984). For this 
reason, poles such as the Easter Island and Dogrib dikes poles 
from the Slave Province (Irving et al. 1984) and the Stillwater 
Complex pole from the Wyoming Province (Geissman and 
Harlan 1988) are omitted from our evaluation, and only poles 
from the Superior Province itself are considered. 
The Matachewan dikes, dated by Heaman (1988) at 2454 2 
2 Ma, yield the most extensively studied and well-defined dual- 
polarity Archean remanence in the Superior Province. Poles 
determined for the dikes by Irving and Naldrett (1977), Shutts 
and Dunlop (1981), Geissman et al. (1983), Ernst and Halls 
(1984), and Halls and Shaw (1988) are all in close agreement 
with the GD pole of this study. This agreement indicates that a 
tectonically stable craton has existed since emplacement of this 
extensive dike swarm and that the postintrusion rotation of 
about 15" between the subterranes across the KSZ, as postulated 
by Bennett et al. (1967), is unlikely. Further, the Matachewan 
poles provided the 2.63 Ga position on the previously published 
APWP's, and it was considered the best-defined Archean result. 
Revision of this position to an age of no more than about 2.45 Ga 
leads to a major revision of the APWP (Fig. 5; Table 3). 
The Matachewan dikes in the Gamitagama greenstone belt 
that were sampled in this study cut the BRQM and have 
the typical north-northwest Matachewan trend and paleomag- 
netic signature that provides a positive contact test. Further, 
Matachewan dikes are known to cut all of the other rock units 
sampled in this study (Ayres 1969; Ernst and Halls 1984), and 
therefore the HSE and NB magnetizations in all probability are 
older than 2.45 Ga. Given that the BRQM and the Northern 
external granite have essentially the same remanence direction 
and U-Pb zircon age, and that this direction fits concordantly on 
the Archean APWP with poles determined from rocks of similar 
age for the Superior Province, it follows that the age of this 
magnetization is >2.45 Ga, the time of Matachewan dike 
intrusion, but <2.66 Ga, which is the U-Pb age of the NB 
group granites. As there is no evidence of a later postintrusive

### page_6
1036 CAN. J. EARTH SCI. VOL. 27, 1990 
FIG. 4. SIRM acquisition and demagnetization curves for example specimens from the (a) HSE group of sites and (b) NB (specimens g and h)

pre-Matachewan thermal remagnetization event, we interpret 
the age of this magnetization as being probably close to the 
maximum U-Pb age of 2.66 Ga (NB; Fig. 5). A similar argument 
holds for the HSE remanence. The three granitic bodies that 
contribute to the HSE pole are physically adjacent and have the 
same magnetization direction, and their pole also fits con- 
cordantly on the APWP. Thus, we interpret the age of this 
remanence as being probably close to that of the latest intrusive 
phase, which is the Southern external granite dated at 2694 Ma 
(Turek et al. 1984) (Fig. 5). This argument for the age of 
magnetization requires that there was no postemplacement tilt in 
the area, which fits with the evidence. Percival and Card (1983) 
argued from regional metamorphic grades that the Wawa area 
could not have been tilted by more than a very few degrees. 
Also, the Matachewan dikes are near vertical in the study area, 
which suggests no postemplacement tilt. 
Across the KSZ to the east in Abitibi Subprovince, Jensen 
and Langford (1983) defined four volcanic cycles that the U-Pb 
zircon dates by Nunes and Jensen (1980), Nunes and Pyke 
(1980), and Corfu et al. (1989) place between 2698 and 
2747 Ma. Thus the maximum age for (i) the Skead volcanics 
pole (SK) is 2701 k 3 Ma; (ii) the Archean basalts and gabbros 
(BG), Kinojevis volcanics (KJ), Ghost Range Complex (GR), 
Adams Mine volcanics and iron formation (AMA), and Dun- 
donald sill (DS) poles is 2706 k 6 Ma; and (iii) the Sherman 
Mines (SMA) and Moose Mountain Mine (MMA) volcanics 
and iron formation poles is 2722 k 20 Ma. Given these 
maximum ages, it is clear that the 2700 Ma positions shown on

Many units providing Archean poles for the Abitibi Sub- 
province have been intruded by undeformed plutons such as the 
Otto Stock and a variety of porphyries that give U-Pb zircon 
ages of 2673:; to 2691 + 3 Ma (Corfu et al. 1989), thereby 
providing one indication of their minimum age of magnetiza- 
tion. In addition, the age date compilation by Easton (1986) 
shows that many whole-rock Rb-Sr isochrons, K-Ar, mineral 
ages, and ''"~rl~~~r plateau ages from these units and later 
undefomed intrusives range from 2450 to 2650 Ma, with several 
ages on crosscutting intrusives of about 2550 Ma. Since these 
ages likely correspond to uplift, they provide a lower limit to the 
ages of magnetizations. All of these units are also cut by the very 
extensive 2454 Ma Matachewan dike swarm, and some positive 
contact tests indicate the host-rock remanence predates their 
emplacement (Irving and Naldrett 1977). Therefore, it is likely 
that the GR, BG, KK, DS, SMA, MMA, and AMA cluster of 
poles (Fig. 5; Table 3), which includes poles from prefolding 
remanences, is older than about 2550 Ma and less than the 
maximum possible age of magnetization from the high-precision 
U-Pb zircon age dates of about 2.7 Ga. Therefore, it is 
reasonable to assign a maximum age of 2.66 Ga to this portion 
of the APWP (Fig. 5), based on the agreement of the NB pole 
from this study with the cluster poles from the Abitibi 
Subprovince. 
Finally, when the HSE, NB, and GD paleopoles determined 
for the Wawa Subprovince in this study are plotted with coeval 
paleopoles from the Superior Province on both sides of the KSZ, 
they appear to be concordant (Fig. 5). Thus, the paleomagnetic 
data to date provide no evidence to indicate any significant 
displacement on the KSZ during the Archean or thereafter. 
However, one must caution that the Archean paleomagnetic 
record for the Superior Province is still sketchy.

### page_8
1038 CAN. J. EARTH SCI. VOL. 27, 1990 
FIG. 5. Archean APWP for Superior Province of North America. 
New poles from this study and their corresponding maximum possible 
ages of magnetization: GD (2.45 Ga), NB (2.66 Ga), and HSE (2.70 
Ga). Circles and triangles are poles determined from the east and west 
side of the Kapuskasing Structural Zone, respectively. See Table 3 for 
pole references. 
Conclusions 
Since the NB and HSE magnetizations are characterized by 
both normal and reverse polarity, this suggests that primary 
remanences have been recorded. The well-defined and charac- 
teristic Matachewan remanence found in the north-northwest- 
trending Gamitagama diabase dikes (GD) constrains the mini- 
mum age of the NB and HSE magnetizations at >2.45 Ga. The 
results from other paleomagnetic studies of the Matachewan 
swarm similarly constrain the minimum age for the rest of the 
prefolding Archean poles in the Superior Province. The 
presence of both polarities, apositive contact test, precise U-Pb 
zircon ages, and the concordancy of the NB and HSE poles with 
the Archean APWP derived from other rock units in other 
subprovinces of the Superior Province are strong arguments in 
favor of our interpretation of the ages of the NB and HSE 
remanences. 
The NB, HSE, and GD paleopoles from this study, combined 
with the revised age for the Matachewan dikes, require revision 
of the APWP for the Superior Province of North America. This 
analysis suggests that no paleomagnetically significant tectonic 
translations or rotations have taken place between the Abitibi 
and Wawa subprovinces on the KSZ since the time of Mata- 
chewan dike intrusion and probably earlier, thus implying that 
a stable craton has existed since the Matachewan dike intrusion. 
Archean apparent polar wander for North America appears to 
have taken place at a very rapid rate, combined with small 
changes in paleolatitudes, suggesting that large-scale rotations 
of the Superior craton took place during the late Archean.
